sources.locator: Relay article read on 2026-10-07 (relay page dated 2018-11-07); the block quote. The EW original was not retrievable.
sources.excerpt: First of all, I was not psychoanalyzed and I hope I never will be. / I'm a very porous person and I absorb a lot of people's feelings. When you're working sometimes with dark subject matter, it can stay with you and then to talk to somebody really nice about it afterwards is a really nice way to move on from the project.
sources.context: Secondary relay of remarks around the Suspiria Venice premiere (September 2018), in which she walked back an earlier report that the film sent her to therapy. Quote only as relayed and attribute to EW.

sources.title: Verity earns $4.5m in previews as Digger trails with $1.2m (The Express Tribune)
sources.speaker: The Express Tribune (entertainment desk)
sources.locator: Full news item read on 2026-10-07.
sources.excerpt: Anne Hathaway and Dakota Johnson's Verity has opened ahead of Tom Cruise's Digger at the domestic box office, earning $4.5 million from Thursday preview screenings. / Verity and Digger are both now playing in cinemas
sources.context: Box-office news item used only to confirm Verity’s release at the start of October 2026. Opening-weekend totals and critical reception were not confirmed from an opened source.

claims.claim: Vogue’s October 2026 cover story says Johnson has developed “a reputation for a certain cool-girl deadpan opacity, a kind of mischievous remove during press appearances.”
claims.passage: for "a certain cool-girl deadpan opacity, a kind of mischievous remove during press appearances."
claims.inference: Establishes the public image the profile tests; it is Vogue’s characterization, not hers.
claims.alternative: A writer’s framing for a cover story; other outlets describe her as candid rather than opaque.

claims.claim: In Architectural Digest’s Open Door video (posted March 11, 2020) she says of a bowl of limes in her kitchen, “They’re great and I love them so much.”
claims.passage: In Architectural Digest's 2020 video tour of her home, she praised a bowl of limes: "They're great and I love them so much."
claims.inference: Even her confession is a bit, and it changes between tellings; the observed pattern is play with a manufactured setup, not a stable factual record of when she learned of the allergy.
claims.alternative: Pure comedy and talk-show craft; it says little about core motive and should not be overread.

claims.claim: On The Tonight Show in January 2021 she said the limes were set dressing, that she is allergic to limes, and “so I just lied. Just lied.”
claims.passage: Ten months later she told Jimmy Fallon the limes had been "set dressing," that she is allergic to them, "so I just lied. Just lied."
claims.inference: Her first account of the limes: a deliberate, pointless put-on.
claims.alternative: Talk-show comedy; the account itself changes later (C51), so it is not a reliable record of when she learned of the allergy.

claims.claim: Asked by Bustle in March 2024, “Is it ever fun to lie to the press though?”, she answered, “The most fun,” and continued, “Sometimes when you’re in a ridiculous situation, you just have to be ridiculous.”
claims.passage: Asked by Bustle in 2024 whether lying to the press is ever fun, she said, "The most fun," and gave her reason: "Sometimes when you're in a ridiculous situation, you just have to be ridiculous."
claims.inference: Her own rule for the put-ons: they are situational play in situations she finds ridiculous, not a general license to deceive.
claims.alternative: A mischievous persona (Seven-like play, counterphobic testing, or survival tactics of a child raised in tabloids) explains this as well as any type; said in an interview she flagged as exaggerated.

claims.claim: In 2026, when the Vogue writer wondered whether her love of passion went against her image of cool remove, the writer saw her “feathers ruffle” for the first time; Johnson answered, “No. I deeply care about a lot of things… I wouldn’t say that I’m cool. What is that, even?… I just want to be authentic… I want to unfold and unfold and really lovingly embrace this life.”
claims.passage: The writer, Alessandra Codinha, wondered whether Johnson's love of passion went against her image of cool remove: "it's the first time I see her feathers ruffle." Johnson answered, "No. I deeply care about a lot of things. I deeply care. I wouldn't say that I'm cool. What is that, even?"
claims.inference: The one moment of visible friction in the latest profile is triggered by being characterized as cool and detached; she corrects the image toward depth of feeling and authenticity.
claims.alternative: Observed and framed by the writer; a single moment in a promotional interview, and “authentic” is common celebrity vocabulary.

claims.claim: After the writer said she didn’t think being cool was necessarily a bad thing, Johnson said, “I just want to be authentic,” and “I want to unfold and unfold and really lovingly embrace this life” (Vogue, 2026).
claims.passage: Codinha said she didn't think being cool was necessarily a bad thing. "I just want to be authentic," Johnson said plainly. "I want to unfold and unfold and really lovingly embrace this life."
claims.inference: She corrects the “cool” image toward authenticity and depth of feeling.
claims.alternative: “Authentic” is common celebrity and indie-producer vocabulary; one exchange in a promotional interview.

claims.claim: In the same March 2024 Bustle interview she said of publicity, “But also, publicly… all that stuff is ridiculous. It’s hard for me to fake it. It’s hard for me sometimes to go along with the silliness of doing a press tour.”
claims.passage: In the same Bustle interview she said, "It's hard for me to fake it. It's hard for me sometimes to go along with the silliness of doing a press tour."
claims.inference: Her “fake it” line is about promotional performance, which is what lets the profile reconcile her put-ons with her authenticity creed.
claims.alternative: Self-report during a press cycle; could also be ordinary celebrity fatigue with press tours.

claims.claim: Interpretation: what she pushes back on repeatedly is having her work turned into something it isn’t.
claims.passage: What she pushes back on, again and again, is having her work turned into something it isn't.
claims.inference: The article’s thesis, built on C07, C25, C28, C37, C74, C75 and C76; narrowed at the edit stage so that the faking-feelings half is stated separately with its Fifty Shades limit (C130).
claims.alternative: See type_hypothesis.against.

claims.claim: Interpretation: Johnson most likely fits Enneagram Type 4 at medium confidence (frontmatter enneagram: 4; title and FAQ).
claims.passage: Dakota Johnson most likely fits Enneagram Type 4, the Individualist, at medium confidence.
claims.inference: The type call that the evidence supports; medium because the discriminator rests largely on promotional self-report.
claims.alternative: Counterphobic Type 6 (C20–C23, C45, C98); Three (C39, C147), Eight, Nine and Seven each explain parts.

claims.claim: Interpretation: across 2015–2026 her most consistent motive is to be met as she actually is and to keep her work from being made into something false.
claims.passage: Across a decade of interviews, what she guards is being met as she actually is, and keeping her work from being made into something false.
claims.inference: Synthesis of C06, C14–C19, C24–C26, C36, C37 and C44; rests mostly on self-report, partly corroborated by Foley (2017), Greeson (2020) and Taylor-Johnson (2017).
claims.alternative: Counterphobic Six (C20–C23, C45), Eight (C09, C13, C34), Nine (C28, C29, C32) and Seven (C11, C12, C33) each explain part of the record; see type_hypothesis.

claims.claim: Interpretation: counterphobic Type 6 is the strongest alternative; Three, Eight, Nine and Seven explain parts of her persona.
claims.passage: An anxious, defiant Type 6 is the strongest alternative; Three, Eight, Nine and Seven each explain pieces of her persona.
claims.inference: Names the alternatives the article tests.
claims.alternative: Ranking of alternatives is itself a judgment.

claims.claim: Dakota Johnson was born on October 4, 1989, in Austin, Texas.
claims.passage: Johnson was born on October 4, 1989, in Austin, Texas
claims.inference: Biographical metadata; Vanity Fair (2022) and Wikipedia agree on the date and place.
claims.alternative: None material. Use the full date only as given; do not add a birth time or hospital.

claims.claim: She is the only child Don Johnson and Melanie Griffith share and one of seven half-siblings in a large blended family (Vanity Fair, 2022); Tippi Hedren is her maternal grandmother.
claims.passage: the only child the actors Don Johnson and Melanie Griffith had together and one of seven half-siblings in a large blended family. The actress Tippi Hedren is her grandmother.
claims.inference: Biographical metadata.
claims.alternative: None material.

claims.claim: Metadata: birth_date 1989-10-04; birth_place Austin, Texas; nationality American; occupation actress and producer.
claims.inference: Vanity Fair (2022) and Wikipedia agree on date and place; Wikipedia gives nationality; AP and Vogue document producing.
claims.alternative: None material.

claims.claim: Vogue (2017) describes her as “born in Texas and raised nowhere in particular,” tagging along on her parents’ film locations, and says she started therapy at age three.
claims.passage: Vogue's 2017 cover story described her as "born in Texas and raised nowhere in particular," trailing her parents to film locations, in therapy from age three
claims.inference: Magazine narration of a rootless childhood.
claims.alternative: Circumstance alone explains rootlessness and later privacy; background, not type evidence.

claims.claim: Vogue (2017) narrates that she had to contend with her parents’ divorce and their “well-publicized struggles with drugs and alcohol.”
claims.passage: contending with their divorce and their "well-publicized struggles with drugs and alcohol."
claims.inference: Sensitive family history, attributed to the magazine, not to her.
claims.alternative: No childhood-wound causation is drawn; these circumstances produce privacy and vigilance regardless of type.

claims.claim: She has said, “I was so consistently unmoored and discombobulated. I didn’t have an anchor anywhere” (2017).
claims.passage: Her own summary: "I was so consistently unmoored and discombobulated. I didn't have an anchor anywhere."
claims.inference: Her own account of an anchorless childhood.
claims.alternative: Background; explains not belonging without any type.

claims.claim: In 2026 she told Vogue school “just became such a dangerous place”; Vogue says this included finding her teacher reading a tabloid detailing her mother’s addiction struggles.
claims.passage: In 2026 she told Vogue that school "just became such a dangerous place," which the magazine says included finding her teacher reading a tabloid about her mother's addiction struggles.
claims.inference: Tabloid exposure reached her as a child; the anecdote is Vogue’s narration.
claims.alternative: Sensitive; attribute to Vogue. Explains privacy and vigilance circumstantially.

claims.claim: Interpretation: a rootless, exposed childhood can produce privacy, vigilance and not belonging in anyone, so it cannot settle her type.
claims.passage: A childhood like that can produce privacy, vigilance and a sense of not belonging in almost anyone, so it can't settle her type.
claims.inference: Guards against childhood-causation reasoning.
claims.alternative: None.

claims.claim: At fashion shows, she said in 2017, she normally sits thinking, “I don’t belong here, I don’t know all these people, I don’t know what I’m talking about.”
claims.passage: At fashion shows, she said in 2017, she normally sits there thinking, "I don't belong here, I don't know all these people, I don't know what I'm talking about."
claims.inference: A recurring outsider feeling; the restored final clause frames it partly as insecurity, not only distinctness.
claims.alternative: A rootless childhood (C02) and social anxiety in crowds (“I’m terrible in crowds”) explain it; the insecurity clause fits a Six as well as a Four.

claims.claim: After high school her father told her to go to college or be cut off financially and “She chose independence” (Vanity Fair, 2022); she took modeling jobs to pay rent while auditioning and broke out with a small role in The Social Network (2010) (Vogue, 2026).
claims.passage: By Vanity Fair's account, after high school her father told her to go to college or be cut off financially, and "She chose independence." She modeled to pay rent while auditioning and landed a small part in David Fincher's _The Social Network_ (2010).
claims.inference: Career-origin facts; “She chose independence” is Vanity Fair’s framing and sits beside the Juilliard rejection (C134) and early industry access (C133), so it is not the whole story.
claims.alternative: Choosing independence over a family ultimatum fits many temperaments (Four, Eight, Seven); use as story, not discriminator.

claims.claim: She calls David Fincher’s remark that her Social Network role “could have easily been thankless and that I did something different with it” “the most wonderful thing anyone’s ever said to me” (2022).
claims.passage: "David said that role could have easily been thankless and that I did something different with it," she said. "I found that to be the most wonderful thing anyone's ever said to me."
claims.inference: The compliment she ranks highest is for being different, not for being good, successful or reliable; a small, telling self-report.
claims.alternative: Any actor would treasure praise from Fincher; the wording of what moved her is the evidence, and it is one remark.

claims.claim: Interpretation: the compliment she ranks highest praises difference, not quality or success.
claims.passage: Not that she was good, or that she had arrived. That she did something different.
claims.inference: Reads the wording of C06.
claims.alternative: One remark; any actor would treasure Fincher’s praise.

claims.claim: Fifty Shades of Grey (2015) and its two sequels made her globally famous, and she publicly defended them for years.
claims.passage: _Fifty Shades of Grey_ (2015) and its two sequels made her world-famous, and for years she defended them.
claims.inference: Career fact plus the dated defenses in C08 and C66.
claims.alternative: None material.

claims.claim: In 2017 she said of Fifty Shades, “I’m truly proud of it… It’s a cool story, and I think it’s different, and different is what I’m about.”
claims.passage: "I'm truly proud of it," she told Vogue in 2017, as the second film came out. "It's a cool story, and I think it's different, and different is what I'm about."
claims.inference: Her earliest stated value in the record is difference; said during the period she later said she could not talk about truthfully (C67), which the article flags (C135).
claims.alternative: Promotional statement during the sequel’s release.

claims.claim: In 2018 she called Fifty Shades “such an incredible platform for me and an incredible experience.”
claims.passage: In 2018 she called the trilogy "such an incredible platform for me and an incredible experience."
claims.inference: Dated continuation of the public defense.
claims.alternative: Press-junket statement.

claims.claim: In 2022 she told Vanity Fair she “signed up to do a very different version of the film we ended up making,” that E.L. James (whose real name, per The Hollywood Reporter, is Erika Mitchell) “had a lot of creative control, all day, every day,” and “It was always a battle. Always.”
claims.passage: In 2022 she told Vanity Fair, "I signed up to do a very different version of the film we ended up making." The author, E.L. James, whose real name is Erika Mitchell, "had a lot of creative control, all day, every day," and "It was always a battle. Always."
claims.inference: Her account of the first film’s creative-control conflict is corroborated by an independent named witness five years earlier; her own rewriting and the sequels rest on her account alone. Shows her fighting to keep the film from becoming something contrived.
claims.alternative: This is an account of a named living person’s conduct; no public response from E.L. James was found. Present it as Johnson’s and Taylor-Johnson’s accounts, keep Johnson’s praise of James, and recheck for a response before publishing.

claims.claim: She said that on set “We’d do the takes of the movie that Erika wanted to make, and then we would do the takes of the movie that we wanted to make,” and that she rewrote scenes the night before.
claims.passage: On set, "We'd do the takes of the movie that Erika wanted to make, and then we would do the takes of the movie that we wanted to make," and she rewrote scenes the night before.
claims.inference: Her account of a named living person’s creative control; “we” is not limited to Dornan.
claims.alternative: No public response from E.L. James found; present as her account.

claims.claim: She said, “I haven’t been able to talk about this truthfully ever, because you want to promote a movie the right way, and I’m proud of what we made ultimately” (2022).
claims.passage: "I haven't been able to talk about this truthfully ever, because you want to promote a movie the right way, and I'm proud of what we made ultimately."
claims.inference: She names the promotional incentive behind her earlier line and, in the same sentence, keeps her pride in the result; the basis for the article’s Fifty Shades test (C148).
claims.alternative: Ordinary press discipline; not evidence of insincerity in either period.

claims.claim: She said of E.L. James, “Erika is a very nice woman, and she was always kind to me and I am grateful she wanted me to be in those movies.”
claims.passage: Of James: "Erika is a very nice woman, and she was always kind to me and I am grateful she wanted me to be in those movies."
claims.inference: Balances the conflict account with praise of James, as the research record requires.
claims.alternative: None.

claims.claim: In June 2017 Sam Taylor-Johnson, director of the first film, said of working with James, who The Hollywood Reporter said had negotiated creative control with Universal, “Her vision versus mine, and they were polar opposite. Every scene was fought over.”
claims.passage: In June 2017, five years before Johnson spoke, Sam Taylor-Johnson said of working with James, who The Hollywood Reporter said had negotiated creative control with Universal, "Her vision versus mine, and they were polar opposite. Every scene was fought over."
claims.inference: Independent named corroboration of the first film’s creative conflict, framed by the director as two opposed visions rather than one-sided obstruction.
claims.alternative: Speaks to the director’s relationship with James, not to Johnson’s rewriting or the sequels.

claims.claim: Taylor-Johnson’s account covers the first film only; Johnson’s rewriting and the sequels rest on her account.
claims.passage: That covers the first film only. Johnson's rewriting and the sequels rest on her word.
claims.inference: States the limit of the corroboration.
claims.alternative: None.

claims.claim: As of October 7, 2026, no public response from E.L. James to Johnson’s 2022 account or Taylor-Johnson’s 2017 account had been found.
claims.passage: As of October 2026 no public response from James to either account had been found.
claims.inference: Research-stage search result.
claims.alternative: A response may exist or appear; absence of a found response is not evidence that none exists.
claims.review_trigger: Recheck for any public response from E.L. James before publishing and at each refresh; add it beside both accounts if found.

claims.claim: In 2024 she said that with Fifty Shades “the author was extremely precious about words, clothing, anything, everything,” and that there was “no room for being expressive or discovering what is present in that real moment that you’re capturing. It’s contrived.”
claims.passage: In 2024 she said the author "was extremely precious about words, clothing, anything, everything," and that there was "no room for being expressive or discovering what is present in that real moment that you're capturing. It's contrived."
claims.inference: Her grievance is contrivance and lost expression, quoted in her own words rather than the draft’s harsher paraphrase.
claims.alternative: Artist rhetoric after a public fallout; still her framing.

claims.claim: She founded TeaTime Pictures in 2019 with former Netflix development executive Ro Donnelly; interviewed at its office in late February 2020, she told Marie Claire, “For a long time, I’d do a movie and have no say.”
claims.passage: In February 2020, at the office of TeaTime Pictures, the production company she had founded in 2019 with the former Netflix executive Ro Donnelly, she told Marie Claire, "For a long time, I'd do a movie and have no say.
claims.inference: A costly, long-term structural choice made so her work would not be turned into something it wasn’t.
claims.alternative: Control and autonomy (Eight) or career strategy (Three) also explain founding a production company; many stars do.

claims.claim: She told Marie Claire (2020), “I could go into something, and it’ll be one thing, and then it comes out as a totally different thing.”
claims.passage: I could go into something, and it'll be one thing, and then it comes out as a totally different thing."
claims.inference: The same grievance as Fifty Shades, generalized; Marie Claire notes she had denied displeasure with Fifty Shades (C147).
claims.alternative: Ordinary actor frustration; career control (Eight/Three) also explains it.

claims.claim: The High Note screenwriter Flora Greeson says Johnson told her, “I don’t want this character apologizing in every scene. That’s not what Maggie does.”
claims.passage: The screenwriter Flora Greeson recalled her note on _The High Note_ (2020): "Dakota was like, 'I don't want this character apologizing in every scene. That's not what Maggie does.'"
claims.inference: A concrete behavioral instance: she defends a character’s right to be openly emotional without apologizing for it.
claims.alternative: Also fits ordinary actorly instinct or a feminist reading of the role; one anecdote.

claims.claim: In a Bustle Q&A published March 5, 2024, answering a question about the film’s nasty reviews, she said she “probably will never do anything like it again because I don’t make sense in that world,” and “That’s why I have my own company. In a movie like that, I have no say about anything.”
claims.passage: Shortly afterward she told Bustle she "probably will never do anything like it again because I don't make sense in that world."
claims.inference: Her grievance is the familiar one (a project becoming something else); her stated plans about such films change with the moment.
claims.alternative: “Along for the ride” is Nine-like passivity; the reversal could be mood, press context or a joke.

claims.claim: In June 2025 she told the Los Angeles Times that “with ‘Madame Web,’ it started out as something and turned into something else. And I was just sort of along for the ride at that point.”
claims.passage: By 2025 she said it had "started out as something and turned into something else. And I was just sort of along for the ride at that point,"
claims.inference: The same grievance a year later.
claims.alternative: “Along for the ride” is also the best Nine evidence (C106).

claims.claim: Interpretation: across a decade her grievance is that what reached the screen stopped being what she signed up to make.
claims.passage: Across a decade, one grievance: what reached the screen stopped being what she signed up to make.
claims.inference: Synthesizes C07, C75, C28, C76.
claims.alternative: Control (Eight) or career strategy (Three) also explain the complaint.

claims.claim: Discussing author involvement in adaptations, she said in 2024, “It’s also about control and feeling powerful, and that’s not what art is.” The article notes this criticizes an author’s control, not her own.
claims.passage: Her line that "It's also about control and feeling powerful, and that's not what art is" was about an author's control, not her own.
claims.inference: Said about someone else’s control; it does not settle her own motive, which the article now states.
claims.alternative: She may want control for herself; her stated remedy is her own company (C139).

claims.claim: She described the TeaTime set to Vogue in 2026 as “womb-like” and “a protective maternal space,” because “I’ve had experiences where people feel forgotten or lost or not taken care of or not seen on set or just undervalued, and I don’t like anyone to feel that way.”
claims.passage: Johnson described the classic TeaTime set to Vogue in 2026 as "womb-like" and "a protective maternal space," because "I've had experiences where people feel forgotten or lost or not taken care of or not seen on set or just undervalued, and I don't like anyone to feel that way."
claims.inference: What she builds when she has power is a place where people are seen; she values the experience of making over output.
claims.alternative: Protectiveness and caretaking also fit Two and Six; this is promotional framing of her company.

claims.claim: She and Cooper Raiff deferred their fees on Cha Cha Real Smooth because the financiers couldn’t afford the costs of making a movie during COVID (Vanity Fair, 2022).
claims.passage: She and the writer-director Cooper Raiff deferred their fees on _Cha Cha Real Smooth_ (2022) because its financiers couldn't cover the extra costs of shooting during COVID.
claims.inference: Costly, sustained effort for small, specific projects she loves; confirmed by several named collaborators.
claims.alternative: Ambition and career strategy explain producing; collaborators are grateful and promotional.

claims.claim: Daddio writer-director Christy Hall says Johnson suggested Sean Penn and that “Within 48 hours, Dakota told me Sean wanted to talk to me”; Penn’s AP account says she knocked on his door with the script.
claims.passage: For _Daddio_ (2024), its writer-director, Christy Hall, says Johnson suggested Sean Penn as her costar: "Within 48 hours, Dakota told me Sean wanted to talk to me."
claims.inference: Two named witnesses confirm her hands-on producing.
claims.alternative: Grateful collaborators in release promotion.

claims.claim: In spring 2026 she produced and starred in Alice Rohrwacher’s Three Incestuous Sisters, shot on Stromboli and in Rome with costars including Saoirse Ronan; Vogue says the film is due in 2027.
claims.passage: In spring 2026 she produced and starred in Alice Rohrwacher's _Three Incestuous Sisters_, shot on Stromboli and in Rome with [Saoirse Ronan](/personality-analysis/saoirse-ronan); Vogue said in 2026 that it was due in 2027.
claims.inference: Current-accuracy facts; not needed for the personality argument.
claims.alternative: Release dates and credits shift.
claims.review_trigger: Recheck when Three Incestuous Sisters gets a release date, premiere or release; update “Vogue said in 2026 that it was due in 2027” and, on release, reopen the type read against the open-section signals (C159).

claims.claim: She said, “When people feel valued and safe to explore their minds, magic happens,” and “The way that it went with Three Sisters, I would be okay if that was the last movie I make” (Vogue, 2026).
claims.passage: "When people feel valued and safe to explore their minds, magic happens," she said. "The way that it went with Three Sisters, I would be okay if that was the last movie I make."
claims.inference: Values the experience of making over output; safety framed as the condition for free exploration.
claims.alternative: Promotional enthusiasm for her own production.

claims.claim: In 2017, responding to tabloid claims that she and Jamie Dornan couldn’t stand each other and were having an affair, she told Vogue, “We hate each other and we’re having an affair, so everybody’s right. How about that?”
claims.passage: In 2017, faced with tabloid claims that she and her costar Jamie Dornan hated each other and were having an affair, she told Vogue, "We hate each other and we're having an affair, so everybody's right. How about that?"
claims.inference: Her press put-ons predate the viral 2019 persona (C141).
claims.alternative: A joke; says little about motive on its own.

claims.claim: On The Ellen DeGeneres Show (aired November 27, 2019), when DeGeneres said she hadn’t been invited to Johnson’s 30th birthday party, Johnson answered, “Actually, no. That’s not the truth, Ellen. You were invited.”
claims.passage: On an episode of _The Ellen DeGeneres Show_ that aired November 27, 2019, [Ellen DeGeneres](/personality-analysis/ellen-degeneres) said she hadn't been invited to Johnson's 30th birthday party. Johnson, laughing, corrected her: "Actually, no. That's not the truth, Ellen. You were invited."
claims.inference: A truthful on-air correction, not a put-on: she declined to go along with a false story about herself even when it was played as a joke. The edit stage moved it out of the put-ons and uses it as their contrast.
claims.alternative: Reads as Eight-like assertion or simple honesty; a Nine reading would expect her to let it slide. One laughing moment; do not overload it. Quote only speaker-unambiguous lines.

claims.claim: Asked about the Ellen exchange in 2024 by an interviewer who praised it (“There’s a special place in heaven for you being on the Ellen show… It was a really winning moment.”), she said, “It will haunt me.”
claims.passage: In 2024, when an interviewer called it "a really winning moment," she said, "It will haunt me."
claims.inference: Wry weariness at being defined by a meme, answering praise; no regret or feud is implied.
claims.alternative: Meaning uncertain; humor.

claims.claim: In January 2021 she told Fallon, “I actually didn’t even know that they were in there,” describing the limes as set dressing.
claims.passage: In January 2021 she told Fallon she "didn't even know that they were in there."
claims.inference: First version of the limes story.
claims.alternative: Comic register.

claims.claim: In December 2021 she said she saw the bowl of limes while filming (“I love them”) and that an allergy test “a few weeks later” showed she is allergic.
claims.passage: By December 2021 she had seen the bowl while filming, and the allergy came from a test "a few weeks later."
claims.inference: Second, different version; the shifting account is the observation.
claims.alternative: Do not treat either version as the factual sequence.

claims.claim: Interpretation: the limes confession is itself a bit and changes between tellings.
claims.passage: Even the confession is a bit, and it changes between tellings.
claims.inference: Compares C49/C50 with C51.
claims.alternative: Talk-show craft; says little about core motive.

claims.claim: Vogue (2026) reports that, according to Johnson, her posture toward the press is “less a ‘bit’ than a survival tactic.”
claims.passage: By 2026, Vogue reported, she saw her posture toward the press as "less a 'bit' than a survival tactic."
claims.inference: Her own framing of the put-ons as defense.
claims.alternative: Fits counterphobic testing or a child raised in tabloids as well as any type.

claims.claim: The Ringer’s Jodi Walker (February 14, 2024), an admirer who loves Johnson “wholeheartedly and fearfully,” wrote that “She will lie—but only at the most unexpected times” and that Johnson lacks the concern other public figures carry “about telling the exact truth about what she thinks and feels in the exact moment.”
claims.passage: Her admirers see no calculation in it. The Ringer's Jodi Walker, who loves her "wholeheartedly and fearfully," wrote that "She will lie—but only at the most unexpected times," and that she lacks the usual worry "about telling the exact truth about what she thinks and feels in the exact moment."
claims.inference: An admiring, non-promotional commentator treats her candor as genuine; the edit stage corrected the draft’s framing of Walker as a skeptic.
claims.alternative: Affectionate commentary, not evidence of motive; the commercial-incentive point is this profile’s own inference (C144).

claims.claim: James Foley, director of Fifty Shades Darker and Freed, told Vogue in 2017, “She has a very sensitive bullshit meter, so if she does something that is the least bit unreal she just stops herself.”
claims.passage: James Foley, who directed the two Fifty Shades sequels, said in 2017, "She has a very sensitive bullshit meter, so if she does something that is the least bit unreal she just stops herself."
claims.inference: A collaborator’s 2017 observation of aversion to the false, predating her later candid persona.
claims.alternative: Director promoting his film; quoted in a flattering profile.

claims.claim: Alessandro Michele, a friend of more than a decade and Gucci’s designer (Vogue, 2017), calls her “the most natural person I have met in this business” (Vogue, 2026); Wikipedia says she has been named a Gucci brand ambassador.
claims.passage: Alessandro Michele, a friend of more than a decade who designed for Gucci, a brand she has represented as an ambassador, calls her "the most natural person I have met in this business."
claims.inference: Friend’s testimony converging with Foley, with his commercial tie disclosed so readers can discount it.
claims.alternative: Interested witness with a business relationship; not independent of S01.

claims.claim: Interpretation: Foley’s 2017 testimony matters most because it predates the candid persona.
claims.passage: Foley's remark matters most because it predates the candid persona.
claims.inference: Dating argument against “authentic is only her later brand.”
claims.alternative: Still one director’s promotional remark.

claims.claim: Interpretation: her line runs between a bit everyone can see is a game and a faked feeling; she has stated the first half herself (C11), the second half is inferred.
claims.passage: So the line, as far as her record shows, runs between a bit, which everyone can see is a game, and a faked feeling.
claims.inference: Labeled in the article as half her own rule, half inference; tested against the Fifty Shades years (C147–C149).
claims.alternative: She may simply enjoy lying; the limes confession itself shifted.

claims.claim: In late February 2020, talking about the COVID-19 scare, she told Marie Claire, “I’m constantly thinking about the state of the world right now. It keeps me up at night, all night, every night.”
claims.passage: In late February 2020, as the COVID-19 scare spread, she told Marie Claire that the state of the world "keeps me up at night, all night, every night."
claims.inference: Real, recurring anxiety, mostly tied to exposure (performing, press scrutiny) and world events.
claims.alternative: Supports a Six reading; also fits social anxiety, a childhood under tabloid scrutiny, and depression. Do not use the L’Officiel “Terrified of what happens to me” line as self-reported fear: in context it is a joke about other actors.

claims.claim: On The Tonight Show in January 2021 she said, “When I come on your show, I get really nervous, and I laugh and then cry most of the time,” and described a panic attack before a singing scene in Our Friend as “like extreme flight mode.”
claims.passage: She told Fallon in 2021 that on his show "I get really nervous, and I laugh and then cry most of the time," and described a panic attack before a singing scene as "like extreme flight mode."
claims.inference: Stage fright and panic in performance settings.
claims.alternative: Common performance anxiety; comic register.

claims.claim: Before the 2026 press tour she said, “everything is watched, and now everyone is a spy, and everyone is the press” (Vogue podcast).
claims.passage: Before her 2026 press tour: "everyone is a spy, and everyone is the press."
claims.inference: Vigilance about exposure.
claims.alternative: Fame explains it for anyone.

claims.claim: In January 2015, relayed from her first Vogue cover story, she said, “I think about my dwindling anonymity, and that’s really scary.”
claims.passage: In January 2015, on the brink of fame, she called her "dwindling anonymity" "really scary."
claims.inference: Consistent across eleven years: exposure feels like a violation of an inner self.
claims.alternative: Fame, a tabloid childhood and ordinary introversion explain privacy for anyone.

claims.claim: In 2026 she told Vogue, “I am obsessed with people not knowing where I am or what I’m doing.”
claims.passage: In 2026: "I am obsessed with people not knowing where I am or what I'm doing."
claims.inference: Privacy, consistent with 2015.
claims.alternative: Fame and a tabloid childhood explain privacy without any type.

claims.claim: In 2017 she said, “A few years ago, I was fighting, waiting for someone to give me a chance. I’m a pretty sensitive person, and when I don’t feel protected, I tend to close right up. But when I feel safe, I think I can do anything.”
claims.passage: In 2017 she said, "A few years ago, I was fighting, waiting for someone to give me a chance. I'm a pretty sensitive person, and when I don't feel protected, I tend to close right up. But when I feel safe, I think I can do anything."
claims.inference: Safety supplied by trusted collaborators, then the ability to act: the shape Six theory predicts. Counted as Six evidence at the edit stage; it does not discriminate for Four.
claims.alternative: A Four also needs safety before opening up; on its own the line fits both readings.

claims.claim: Explaining “The blood of the covenant is thicker than the water of the womb” in 2024, she said it means “the connections with people you choose are more solid than the connections to the people you’re actually born to.”
claims.passage: She prizes chosen family, too: "the connections with people you choose are more solid than the connections to the people you're actually born to."
claims.inference: Loyalty to a chosen circle, voiced by someone who grew up among seven half-siblings (C59).
claims.alternative: Loyalty is central to the Six alternative; her large blended family explains it circumstantially.

claims.claim: In a jokey 2024 Bustle Q&A she called herself “a real sucker. I would be the first one to join a cult,” and, asked which cult, named any that promised “this will make you a better person for other people.” In a separate answer, after the interviewer called her persona anti-authoritarian, she said, “I am a very defiant person. If somebody tells me I can’t do something, I am shaking, even if I had no interest in doing that thing.”
claims.passage: She called herself "a real sucker. I would be the first one to join a cult," and, asked which one, named any that promised "this will make you a better person for other people." In a separate answer, after the interviewer called her persona anti-authoritarian, she said, "I am a very defiant person. If somebody tells me I can't do something, I am shaking, even if I had no interest in doing that thing."
claims.inference: Two separate joking answers; the authority contrast was the interviewer’s. Read literally, reflexive defiance looks counterphobic.
claims.alternative: She flagged exaggeration in this interview; Fours resisting definition, Eights and Sevens predict the same defiance.

claims.claim: Interpretation: read literally the defiance looks counterphobic, but it comes from an interview she flagged as exaggerated and other types predict it, so it does not discriminate.
claims.passage: Read literally, that reflex looks counterphobic. But it comes from the interview she said she exaggerated in, and a Four resisting being defined, an Eight or a Seven could say the same.
claims.inference: Reclassifies the defiance as non-discriminating instead of a Six signature left unanswered.
claims.alternative: A Six reader may still weight it; the article keeps it in the Six case.

claims.claim: Describing what she and Maggie Gyllenhaal let go of on The Lost Daughter, she said, “It’s this fear of when you have the potential to do things, but you’re just like, is that going to be okay?” and of Gyllenhaal, “She kind of was my shepherd in that way” (2021).
claims.passage: Of _The Lost Daughter_, she said, "It's this fear of when you have the potential to do things, but you're just like, is that going to be okay?" Its director, Maggie Gyllenhaal, "kind of was my shepherd in that way."
claims.inference: Doubt-and-permission language plus a trusted guide: the best single passage for the Six case.
claims.alternative: She frames the fear as an obstacle to becoming her fullest self, which a Four reading can absorb.

claims.claim: On Materialists she “felt like I was in such good hands, I could just relax into that role” (2025).
claims.passage: On _Materialists_ (2025): "I felt like I was in such good hands, I could just relax into that role."
claims.inference: She can cede control when she trusts the filmmaker.
claims.alternative: Fits Nine ease or Six trust in a good authority; argues against a pure Eight reading.

claims.claim: Interpretation: the Six case (anxiety, vigilance, loyalty, ambivalence toward authority, trusted guide) is why confidence is medium.
claims.passage: Anxiety, vigilance, loyalty, ambivalence toward authority, a trusted guide through fear: this is why the Four reading is held at medium confidence.
claims.inference: Summarizes C20–C23, C29, C45, C90–C92.
claims.alternative: None.

claims.claim: Interpretation: the discriminator is what her fights are about. A Six’s grievance is usually broken trust; Johnson tells hers as lost expression (“no room for being expressive,” “It’s contrived,” “that’s not what art is”).
claims.passage: What separates the readings is what her fights are about. A Six's grievance is usually broken trust: an authority who misled her or left her exposed. Johnson's could be told that way, but she tells it as lost expression: "no room for being expressive," "It's contrived," "that's not what art is."
claims.inference: Replaces the draft’s safety-as-precondition test, which reviewers showed fits a Six. Grounded in C07, C74, C75, C76, C79 and C37 across 2017–2025; Taylor-Johnson independently frames the Fifty Shades fight as opposed visions.
claims.alternative: A Six could also feel the work was taken from her; the framing is her own, given in interviews, and “authentic/expressive” is industry vocabulary.
claims.review_trigger: Recheck at each refresh, on the release of Three Incestuous Sisters, and whenever a non-promotional long-form account appears: if she describes a production conflict as being misled or left unprotected, weigh it toward Six; if as the work being made false, toward Four.

claims.claim: Recalling learning at 10 that the Easter Bunny didn’t exist, she said in 2022, “But if I could, I would still believe in it now. Maybe that’s why I make movies and why I want to make movies forever and ever. It makes things feel a little bit more safe.”
claims.passage: Even moviemaking serves safety. Recalling learning at 10 that the Easter Bunny wasn't real, she said in 2022, "But if I could, I would still believe in it now. Maybe that's why I make movies and why I want to make movies forever and ever. It makes things feel a little bit more safe."
claims.inference: In this line belief and moviemaking serve safety; the edit stage moved it from the Four side to the Six case.
claims.alternative: A light anecdote about enchantment; a Four could also treat make-believe as refuge.

claims.claim: She said of choosing projects in 2020, “I really don’t have a method, and I don’t want one… It’s very intuitive and emotional.”
claims.passage: "I really don't have a method, and I don't want one," she said of choosing projects in 2020. "It's very intuitive and emotional."
claims.inference: Decisions run on feeling and taste rather than systems, guidance or rules.
claims.alternative: A Seven or Nine could also resist method; producers often say this in interviews.

claims.claim: She said in 2024, “I think I just find rules and some structure really ridiculous, silly and stupid,” and told Vogue in 2026, “Rules are really tough for me.”
claims.passage: Rules are "really ridiculous, silly and stupid" (Bustle, 2024) and "really tough for me" (Vogue, 2026).
claims.inference: Resistance to rules corroborated across two outlets and years.
claims.alternative: Counterphobic Six (reflexive defiance of authority), Eight (autonomy) and Nine (accommodate, then quietly do your own thing) all fit parts of this.

claims.claim: She said in 2024, “Everyone who makes decisions is afraid. They want to do the safe thing, and the safe thing is really boring.”
claims.passage: Decision-makers, she said in 2024, "want to do the safe thing, and the safe thing is really boring."
claims.inference: She disdains safety-seeking and control in creative decisions, the opposite of what a security-first motive would defend.
claims.alternative: Common artist rhetoric during a bad box-office moment; also fits Eight anti-control sentiment.

claims.claim: She has struggled with depression since she was “15 or 14” and says “I am in a lot of therapy” (Marie Claire, 2020); she is “always trying to navigate that in an honest and safe way” (Vanity Fair, 2022); Vogue (2026) writes that “Various modalities of therapy have helped,” as has “a solid network of friends and chosen family.”
claims.passage: She is open about depression, which she dates to "15 or 14," and about the help she gets: "I am in a lot of therapy" (Marie Claire, 2020); "I'm always trying to navigate that in an honest and safe way" (Vanity Fair, 2022). Vogue wrote in 2026 that "Various modalities of therapy have helped," as has "a solid network of friends and chosen family."
claims.inference: First-person mental-health history with the professional and personal support she credits in all three sources. Not used as type evidence.
claims.alternative: Depression can mimic Four melancholy; the article states it is not type evidence (C154). Wikipedia’s unsourced rehabilitation claim is not used.

claims.claim: Of a scarab tattoo, a symbol of rebirth, she said in 2022, “I think that’s been me forever,” and, reading that Roe v. Wade was likely to be overturned, “if I didn’t try and apply great meaning to little things, I honestly don’t think I’d make it.”
claims.passage: Of a scarab tattoo, a symbol of rebirth, she said in 2022, "I think that's been me forever." Reading that spring that Roe v. Wade was likely to be overturned, she said, "if I didn't try and apply great meaning to little things, I honestly don't think I'd make it."
claims.inference: A habit of symbolic meaning-making; a lean toward Four, not a separation.
claims.alternative: The scarab line sits in the same breath as her therapy and depression remarks; a Six can anchor in belief too.

claims.claim: She said she felt like her Lost Daughter character, Nina, “so hungry and so thirsty for something else and to be seen—to not just be the hot girl on the beach,” adding, “I feel like that in my career a lot” (2021).
claims.passage: She related to her _Lost Daughter_ character, "so hungry and so thirsty for something else and to be seen—to not just be the hot girl on the beach," adding, "I feel like that in my career a lot."
claims.inference: Names being seen accurately, beyond surface image, as a career-long hunger and as the basis of trust.
claims.alternative: Awards-campaign talk about a role; actors routinely identify with characters. The specificity (“the hot girl on the beach,” trust built on not being seen) is the evidence.

claims.claim: She said she trusted Gyllenhaal “because I knew that she knows what it feels like to not be seen” (2021).
claims.passage: Even the "shepherd" trust rested on being seen: she trusted Gyllenhaal "because I knew that she knows what it feels like to not be seen."
claims.inference: The trust behind the Six-case “shepherd” line rests on being seen.
claims.alternative: The same answer adds “She knows what it feels like to not be handled with grace and with care,” which is protection language a Six reading can claim.

claims.claim: Interpretation: the Fincher compliment, the TeaTime set and the “cool” bristle share one theme, being seen accurately.
claims.passage: Fincher's compliment, the TeaTime set where no one goes unseen, the bristle at "cool": the theme holds.
claims.inference: Links C06, C26, C14.
claims.alternative: Three moments; self-report.

claims.claim: Richard E. Grant said in 2022 that “having seen her on that infamous Ellen DeGeneres interview, you know that she takes no prisoners.”
claims.passage: which led her _Persuasion_ costar Richard E. Grant to say in 2022, "you know that she takes no prisoners."
claims.inference: A forceful public presence, partly derived from the Ellen clip (Grant says so).
claims.alternative: Fits Eight; much of it is costar warmth in promotional contexts.

claims.claim: Anne Hathaway, her Verity costar, said in 2026, “She’s actually very cozy and lovable, but she has, unmistakably, very, very powerful jungle cat energy.”
claims.passage: [Anne Hathaway](/personality-analysis/anne-hathaway), her _Verity_ costar, said in 2026 that she is "very cozy and lovable, but she has, unmistakably, very, very powerful jungle cat energy."
claims.inference: Forceful presence, with warmth.
claims.alternative: Costar promoting the same film.

claims.claim: In 2017 she said that after two years of exposure she went into “this weird K-hole of feeling so scared of people” and became “shut off to strangers, even cold. That’s not my nature. I prefer to be tender”; Vogue reported in 2017 that tender is her favorite word and tattooed on her forearm.
claims.passage: In 2017 she described "feeling so scared of people" after early fame and becoming "shut off to strangers, even cold. That's not my nature. I prefer to be tender." Vogue reported that year that tender was her favorite word, tattooed on her forearm.
claims.inference: Volunteered vulnerability, with the fear clause restored at the edit stage; dated to 2017.
claims.alternative: Fear of people also feeds the Six case; an Eight can admit softness privately, but these are public admissions.

claims.claim: She said in 2018, as relayed from Entertainment Weekly, “I’m a very porous person and I absorb a lot of people’s feelings.”
claims.passage: In 2018: "I'm a very porous person and I absorb a lot of people's feelings."
claims.inference: Volunteered permeability, repeated as “porous” in 2026.
claims.alternative: Secondary relay of EW.

claims.claim: She said in 2024, “I can be out at my house and not see or speak to another human for days on end, and I feel wonderful.”
claims.passage: "I can be out at my house and not see or speak to another human for days on end, and I feel wonderful," she said in 2024.
claims.inference: Withdrawal and rest are restorative for her.
claims.alternative: Strongest support for a Nine or withdrawn reading; depression and exhausting schedules also explain it.

claims.claim: She calls her home life “Just low-key” (Vogue, 2026).
claims.passage: In 2026 she called her home life "Just low-key."
claims.inference: Restorative quiet.
claims.alternative: Fits Nine; also ordinary.

claims.claim: On Madame Web she was “just sort of along for the ride” (2025).
claims.passage: On _Madame Web_ she was "along for the ride."
claims.inference: Nine-like passivity in one project.
claims.alternative: Could be resignation on a studio film.

claims.claim: In 2017 she said, “I think I’m a little bit heartbroken all the time, even when I’m in a happy relationship. I don’t do casual very well, and my feelings, even the good ones, get so intense that they hurt.”
claims.passage: "I think I'm a little bit heartbroken all the time, even when I'm in a happy relationship. I don't do casual very well, and my feelings, even the good ones, get so intense that they hurt."
claims.inference: Longing and heightened feeling as a standing condition rather than a reaction to events, stated nine years apart.
claims.alternative: Depression (C04) and an actor’s trained emotional access can produce the same language.

claims.claim: Her friend Talia Bernstein says, “She’s sillier than most people know… I’ve been at so many small gatherings with her where she’s putting on a dance or changing into a costume…. She likes to laugh” (Vogue, 2026).
claims.passage: "She's sillier than most people know," says her friend, the writer Talia Bernstein. "I've been at so many small gatherings with her where she's putting on a dance or changing into a costume…. She likes to laugh."
claims.inference: A strong playful, mischievous streak that coexists with the melancholy self-description.
claims.alternative: Fits Seven; the melancholy-only Four stereotype does not predict it.

claims.claim: On a 2026 Vogue podcast she joked that she and Jennifer Lawrence “could be the ultimate internet trolls if we, A, had the time and, B, the interest.”
claims.passage: On a 2026 Vogue podcast, she joked that she and [Jennifer Lawrence](/personality-analysis/jennifer-lawrence) "could be the ultimate internet trolls if we, A, had the time and, B, the interest."
claims.inference: Mischief.
claims.alternative: A joke.

claims.claim: Asked about motherhood in 2024, she said, “I really want to experience everything that life has to offer,” and a few sentences later, “There’s so much to eat up and learn and grow from and experience and feel. That includes all the pain and the suffering and feeling so helpless about the world.”
claims.passage: Asked about motherhood in 2024, she said she wants "to experience everything that life has to offer," which is close to a Seven's motto. A few sentences later: "That includes all the pain and the suffering and feeling so helpless about the world."
claims.inference: Unlike a Seven’s appetite, hers explicitly embraces suffering and self-reproach as part of what she wants to feel.
claims.alternative: Read alone, “experience everything” is Seven language; the second half is what separates it.

claims.claim: She said in 2017, “The stories I want to tell, the characters I want to play, don’t typically exist in huge, commercial box-office movies… But this is a business.”
claims.passage: She is frank about commerce: the stories and characters she wants "don't typically exist in huge, commercial box-office movies," she said in 2017. "But this is a business."
claims.inference: Commercial calculation that supports a Three reading; the same sentence names non-commercial taste.
claims.alternative: Supports a Three or practical-careerist reading of some choices; tempers the purist image.

claims.claim: In March 2024 she said she probably would never do anything like Madame Web again; in June 2025, “There’s no part of me that’s like, ‘Oh, I’ll never do that again’ to anything. I’ve done even tiny movies that didn’t do well. Who cares?”
claims.passage: and she had dropped the vow: "There's no part of me that's like, 'Oh, I'll never do that again' to anything. I've done even tiny movies that didn't do well. Who cares?"
claims.inference: Stated plans change with the moment; the shrug at films that “didn’t do well” cuts against an image-protecting Three reading (C155) and against reputational distancing as the whole story (C140).
claims.alternative: Press context or a joke.

claims.claim: Interpretation: her anxiety is high for a Four, and depression can mimic Four melancholy.
claims.passage: Her anxiety runs high for a Four, and the depression she describes can resemble Four melancholy without being a personality trait.
claims.inference: Counterevidence and a diagnosis-vs-personality caution.
claims.alternative: None.

claims.claim: Sam Taylor-Johnson and The Ringer are the only sources here from outside her promotional circle; neither speaks to her motives, and no skeptical account of her motives was found.
claims.passage: Taylor-Johnson and The Ringer are the only voices here from outside her promotional circle; neither speaks to her motives, and no skeptical account of them turned up.
claims.inference: Source-limit statement.
claims.alternative: None.
claims.review_trigger: Recheck at each refresh for a critical or non-promotional account of her as a producer or collaborator; add it beside the type argument if found.

claims.claim: The July 2026 Vogue interview was timed to Verity, a thriller costarring Anne Hathaway, which opened at the start of October 2026; Johnson was 36 at the time.
claims.passage: In July 2026, in an interview for Vogue's October cover timed to the thriller _Verity_ ([released that October](https://tribune.com.pk/story/2632636/verity-earns-45m-in-previews-as-digger-trails-with-12m)), Johnson, then 36, talked about slowing down
claims.inference: Dated context only; not needed for the argument.
claims.alternative: Release details shift.

claims.claim: Vogue reports that when filming ends and everyone goes home, she finds it “shattering,” and she said, “I’ve felt that sort of heartbreak I don’t even know how many times now in my life… It’s like leaving summer camp. It’s so devastating. And I don’t know how much more heartbreak my heart can handle.”
claims.passage: When a film wraps and everyone goes home, Vogue reports, she finds it "shattering." "I've felt that sort of heartbreak I don't even know how many times now in my life," she said. "It's like leaving summer camp. It's so devastating. And I don't know how much more heartbreak my heart can handle."
claims.inference: Intense, recurring grief at the end of a shoot; she presents it as a thing that happens on set, not as unique to her.
claims.alternative: Common among actors; depression also colors it.

claims.claim: Vogue says the Stromboli shoot was the kind of thing she joined the industry to be part of: “a safe container full of artists feeling free.”
claims.passage: the kind of set Vogue says she joined the industry for, "a safe container full of artists feeling free."
claims.inference: Vogue’s phrase, attributed as such.
claims.alternative: The writer’s framing.

claims.claim: Interpretation: wrap grief is common and a Six could mourn a lost secure group; what is specific is how often she says it has happened and what ends each time.
claims.passage: Plenty of actors grieve a wrap, and a Six could mourn the loss of a secure group. What is specific to her telling is the count and what ends each time
claims.inference: Replaces the draft’s unsupported “most actors” contrast.
claims.alternative: Actors commonly grieve wrap; the Six reading of a lost secure group is stated in the passage.

claims.claim: She said in July 2026, “Maybe spending a little bit more time just existing as a human is what I’ll be doing.”
claims.passage: "Maybe spending a little bit more time just existing as a human is what I'll be doing."
claims.inference: Dated closing statement.
claims.alternative: Plans change.
claims.review_trigger: Recheck at each refresh against her announced projects; the sentence is dated to July 2026 and is no longer the article’s closing line.

claims.claim: Description: she calls lying to the press “the most fun” yet says “It’s hard for me to fake it.”
claims.passage: Dakota Johnson calls lying to the press "the most fun" yet says "It's hard for me to fake it."
claims.inference: Both lines from the same March 2024 Bustle interview.
claims.alternative: See C15.

claims.claim: Title: she is a prankster who says it is hard for her to fake it (her own words, Bustle 2024).
claims.passage: Dakota Johnson: The Prankster Who Says It's Hard to Fake It
claims.inference: Mirrors C15 in her own wording rather than asserting the article’s inference as a trait; the body tests it against the Fifty Shades years (C147–C149).
claims.alternative: An inference, labeled as such in the body.

claims.claim: FAQ: Type 4 leads over 6 because her grievances are framed as the work being made false (“no room for being expressive”) rather than betrayal, and because she says she hungers “to be seen.”
claims.passage: Type 4 leads because of what her fights are about: she describes troubled films as the work being made false, with "no room for being expressive," rather than as a betrayal, and what she says she hungers for is "to be seen."
claims.inference: Mirrors C95 and C16.
claims.alternative: See type_hypothesis.alternative_case.

claims.claim: FAQ: Sam Taylor-Johnson said in 2017, “Every scene was fought over.”
claims.passage: In 2017 the film's director, Sam Taylor-Johnson, said "Every scene was fought over."
claims.inference: Mirrors C72.
claims.alternative: First film only.

claims.claim: FAQ: she said she was “proud of what we made ultimately,” does not regret Fifty Shades, and called James “a very nice woman.”
claims.passage: She also said she was "proud of what we made ultimately," that she does not regret it, and that James is "a very nice woman."
claims.inference: Mirrors C67, C136 and C71.
claims.alternative: None.

claims.claim: FAQ: DeGeneres conceded she remembered being invited.
claims.passage: DeGeneres conceded she remembered being invited.
claims.inference: Mirrors C09.
claims.alternative: None.

claims.claim: FAQ: limes accounts in January and December 2021.
claims.passage: In January 2021 she told Jimmy Fallon the limes in her 2020 Architectural Digest home tour were set dressing, that she is allergic, and "I just lied." In December 2021 she said "I love them" and that she learned of the allergy from a test "a few weeks later."
claims.inference: Mirrors C49–C51 and presents the shifting account.
claims.alternative: Neither version is treated as the factual sequence.

claims.claim: FAQ: TeaTime Pictures was founded in 2019 with former Netflix development executive Ro Donnelly.
claims.passage: TeaTime Pictures, which she founded in 2019 with former Netflix development executive Ro Donnelly.
claims.inference: Wikipedia (citing Deadline, October 2019) and Bustle name Donnelly; Marie Claire interviewed her at the TeaTime office in February 2020.
claims.alternative: None.
claims.review_trigger: Recheck TeaTime’s status, cofounder and ownership at each refresh and whenever a TeaTime production is announced or released.

claims.claim: FAQ: TeaTime’s early productions included Cha Cha Real Smooth (2022) and Daddio (2024); in 2026 she described its sets as “a protective maternal space.”
claims.passage: Its early productions included Cha Cha Real Smooth (2022) and Daddio (2024), and in 2026 she described its sets as "a protective maternal space."
claims.inference: Vanity Fair, AP and Vogue list both as TeaTime films.

type_hypothesis.against: Real evidence resists Type 4. (1) Anxiety and fear recur: COVID-era anxiety that kept her up “all night, every night” (2020), stage fright and a panic attack before a singing scene, “everyone is a spy” before the 2026 press tour, and “feeling so scared of people” after early fame (C21, C90, C91, C35); she names her own fear of “is that going to be okay?” and calls Gyllenhaal her “shepherd” (C45), relaxes when “in such good hands” (C29) and values chosen-family loyalty (C23). (2) Her safety language fits a Six: in 2017 protection from collaborators who “give me a chance” comes first and the freedom to act follows (C20, C150), and in 2022 she said moviemaking itself “makes things feel a little bit more safe” (C98); on safety talk alone the Six reading wins (C151). (3) The Bustle defiance (“I am shaking, even if I had no interest”) reads counterphobic if taken literally (C22, C93). (4) Three: she is frank that “this is a business” (C39), held an on-message Fifty Shades line for years and reportedly denied displeasure (C08, C66, C147), and her grievances arrive after films are finished or panned, which fits reputational distancing (C140). (5) The public persona reads as Eight (Ellen correction, “takes no prisoners,” “jungle cat energy,” defiance, her own company: C09, C34, C102, C22, C139); Nine (days alone, “Just low-key,” “along for the ride”: C32, C105, C106); Seven (play, costumes, trolling, “The most fun”: C33, C109, C11). (6) Incentives and circumstance: “authentic” is industry vocabulary; a rootless, tabloid-exposed childhood (C02, C03, C62) explains privacy and not belonging without any type; lifelong depression (C04) can mimic Four melancholy and is not used as evidence. (7) Source limits: nearly all testimony comes from friends and collaborators in promotional pieces; Taylor-Johnson (S35) and The Ringer (S38) are the only voices outside that circle, neither speaks to motive, and The Ringer is admiring, not skeptical (C113).
type_hypothesis.alternative_case: Counterphobic Type 6 is the strongest rival. She reports recurring anxiety and fear (C21, C90, C91, C35) and doubt about whether acting on her potential is “going to be okay?” (C45); her safety talk credits trusted others before she can act (“waiting for someone to give me a chance… when I feel safe, I think I can do anything,” C20) and even frames moviemaking as what “makes things feel a little bit more safe” (C98); she values loyalty to a chosen circle (C23), works best with directors who make her feel in “good hands” (C29) and calls Gyllenhaal her “shepherd” (C45); she distrusts executives and the press (C153, C30, C84); and, read literally, her reflexive defiance (“I am shaking, even if I had no interest”) and joking suggestibility (“the first one to join a cult”) fit a Six’s split with authority (C22). Building TeaTime as “a protective maternal space” (C26) fits a security-driven core as well. Type 3 is a real second rival (commercial frankness, years on message: C39, C147, C140); Type 8 explains the Ellen correction, defiance and her company (C09, C22, C34, C102, C139); Type 9 explains withdrawal and “along for the ride” (C32, C105, C106); Type 7 explains her mischief and appetite for experience (C11, C33, C109, C44) but not her dwelling in pain.
type_hypothesis.discriminator: What her fights are about, not how much she needs safety (safety-as-precondition fits a Six and is conceded in C150–C151). A Six’s grievance is usually broken trust: an authority who misled her or left her exposed. Johnson tells her grievances, across a decade, as lost expression: Fifty Shades left “no room for being expressive… It’s contrived” (C74), control “is not what art is” (C79), films come out “a totally different thing” (C75), Madame Web “turned into something else” (C76), executives deciding “what is going to work in an artistic sense doesn’t actually make sense to me” (C153), and her High Note note defended a character’s right not to apologize (C37, C152); Sam Taylor-Johnson independently frames the first film’s fight as opposed visions (C72). Supporting tilts, none decisive: she wants “to be seen—to not just be the hot girl on the beach” and trusted Gyllenhaal because “she knows what it feels like to not be seen” (C16, C100); the compliment she ranks highest is for doing “something different” (C06); being called cool is the one thing that ruffles her (C14); she rejects method and rules across outlets (C24, C13) and scorns “the safe thing” (C30), which counterphobic Sixes also do; she reads her life symbolically (C19). Against Three: she punctures her own image in public (doesn’t “make sense” in that world, shrugs at flops, would accept a small film as her last: C28, C111, C82, C155). Against Eight: she volunteers fear and tenderness (C35, C103). Against Nine: standing intense feeling (C18). Against Seven: her appetite explicitly includes “the pain and the suffering” (C44). Foley’s 2017 testimony predates the viral 2019 persona (C36, C141). The discriminator rests largely on self-report in promotional settings, hence medium confidence.
type_hypothesis.unexplained: The Fifty Shades years: warm promotion (2017, 2018) and a reported 2020 denial of displeasure (C147), followed by the 2022 account she said she could not give “truthfully” before (C67); the article reads this as withholding the fight rather than faking pride (C148), but the denial’s wording is unknown (C156) and a Three or loyal Six reading also fits. Her relish for put-ons (“The most fun”; the shifting limes confession) in someone who says “It’s hard for me to fake it” (C11, C15, C52); the bit/feeling line is half her own rule, half inference (C145). The Madame Web reversal (C28, C111). The slapstick, costume-party sociability friends describe (C33). Anxiety and self-doubt that are high for a Four (C21, C45, C112). Whether her defiance is temperament or a learned response to a childhood in the tabloids. Wing and instinctual subtype are not established.
